confounds: The set is highly imbalanced: 618 diagnosed users versus 5,464 controls, with rare-event estimates especially sensitive to a small number of prolific users.

Diagnosed users were generally more prolific: fold-level median timelines were about 337-469 posts versus 324.5-344 for controls, so user-level prevalence is exposure-sensitive even when post shares are reported.

Topic mixtures differ sharply: diagnosed users show more fandom/pop-culture content, while controls show more politics/news; these patterns may reflect age, gender, interests, source selection, or batch composition.
There are no timestamps, so repeated posts indicate recurrence within a retained timeline, not persistence over days or weeks.
Self-versus-other, quotation, lyric, irony, and joke distinctions were heuristic; no manual semantic annotation was available.
Treatment and diagnosis disclosure may reflect healthcare access, willingness to self-disclose, or annotation rules rather than latent depression itself.

caveats: Context classification is heuristic and not manually validated.
Distinct-post persistence is not duration or clinical severity.
findings.evidence_summary: Among mental-health posts, first-person/context cues occurred in 64.1% of diagnosed versus 43.2% of control posts; nonpersonal markers occurred in 18.2% versus 30.2%. Repetition across distinct posts strengthened the difference.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prefer specific first-person experience, persistence, and co-occurring impairment or care language; downweight isolated keywords, quotations, jokes, lyrics, advocacy, and third-person discussion.

quantitative_support.effect: +31.3 percentage points; fold range +26.1 to +34.6 pp
quantitative_support.measure: users with at least one self/context-filtered mental-health post
users with at least two distinct filtered posts

findings.signal: Self-referential, non-quoted, non-joking mental-health narratives are substantially more associated with diagnosed labels than isolated topic words.

caveats: Treatment may concern other conditions or someone else.
Healthcare access, disclosure, and annotation practices may confound the association.
findings.evidence_summary: The association remains positive in all four folds and is stronger when treatment references are first-person and repeated. Psychiatrist mentions were 13.1% of diagnosed users versus 3.2% of controls.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use treatment as supporting evidence only when self-experienced and specific; combine with mental-health or impairment context.

quantitative_support.effect: +27.6 percentage points; fold range +22.4 to +34.0 pp
quantitative_support.measure: users with at least one personal treatment/medication post
users with at least two such posts

findings.signal: Personal therapy, psychiatric care, medication, and treatment-management language is a robust semantic cluster.

caveats: The lexical screen can capture non-depression diagnoses and generic diagnostic discussion.
findings.evidence_summary: Self-referential diagnosis wording, medical labels, and code-like references show a small, consistent excess, but the signal is much rarer than general mental-health discussion.
findings.prompt_guidance: Treat explicit diagnosis language as high-specificity supporting evidence only when it clearly refers to the author and aligns with psychiatric or treatment context.

quantitative_support.effect: +2.2 percentage points; fold range +1.5 to +3.4 pp
quantitative_support.measure: users triggering a narrow self/diagnosis-language screen

findings.signal: Explicit diagnostic or medical-code framing is rare but elevated among diagnosed users.

caveats: Keyword presence substantially overstates personal risk.
No manual intent annotation was available.
findings.evidence_summary: The user-level and post-level excess is stable across folds, yet many mentions are figurative, humorous, media-related, advocacy-oriented, or about other people.
findings.prompt_guidance: Require self-directed intent or personal experience, exclude quotation/news/fiction/jokes, and never treat this as a standalone clinical conclusion.
findings.signal: Suicide and self-harm topics are elevated, but their semantic interpretation must be highly context-sensitive.

caveats: Ordinary academic stress, employment loss, age, and socioeconomic conditions can produce the same wording.
findings.evidence_summary: Generic work or school topics were nearly universal; the useful distinction was concrete disruption or inability rather than merely mentioning the domain.
findings.prompt_guidance: Look for explicit first-person inability, absence, abandonment, or loss of functioning, preferably repeated or linked to mental-health/treatment context.

quantitative_support.effect: +7.4 percentage points; fold range +4.2 to +11.3 pp
quantitative_support.measure: users with specific work/study impairment wording

findings.signal: Specific inability to study, work, attend, or maintain school/work commitments is a modest but stable diagnosed-associated signal.

caveats: The lexicons include ordinary tiredness, pain, sleep, and eating talk.
Physical illness and routine lifestyle differences are plausible confounds.
findings.evidence_summary: User-level prevalence is higher, but post-normalized differences are small and sometimes near zero; broad symptom words are common in both groups.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use only as secondary evidence when symptoms are self-experienced, specific, and persistent.
findings.signal: Sleep, fatigue, appetite, and physical-symptom language is only weakly elevated.

caveats: Irony, relationship talk, ordinary frustration, and platform-wide expressive language are common.
findings.evidence_summary: The diagnosed group more often contains at least one such post, but isolation language is close to null after accounting for post frequency and generic loneliness terms are widespread.
findings.prompt_guidance: Do not rely on single words such as alone, empty, tired, or hopeless; require first-person specificity, persistence, and corroborating impairment or care evidence.
findings.signal: Negative affect and isolation show user-level excesses but weak, non-specific post-normalized separation.

caveats: Future verbs and goals can be routine, performative, or unrelated to wellbeing.
The corpus has no reliable chronology for evaluating sustained hope or follow-through.
findings.evidence_summary: Planning language was slightly more frequent in the diagnosed group across all folds, providing counterevidence against treating future orientation absence as a general label cue.
findings.prompt_guidance: Do not infer control status from future planning or diagnosed status from its absence; interpret plans alongside affect and functioning.
findings.signal: Future plans, goals, and concrete intentions were not suppressed in diagnosed users.

caveats: Observed social activity online does not measure offline isolation or relationship quality.
findings.evidence_summary: Both groups discuss friends, family, romance, outings, and social activities extensively; the small diagnosed excess is not substantively diagnostic.
findings.prompt_guidance: Avoid interpreting ordinary relational or social-topic presence as evidence for either label.
findings.signal: Relationships and social participation do not meaningfully separate the labels in this corpus.

caveats: Humor can coexist with distress and is highly platform- and subculture-dependent.
findings.evidence_summary: Diagnosed users have slightly higher user-level exposure, consistent with longer timelines, but controls have slightly higher average humor post share overall.
findings.prompt_guidance: Do not equate humor absence with depression or humor presence with control status.

quantitative_support.effect: 0.87-1.03x post-rate ratio by fold; mixed direction

findings.signal: Humor and laughter are common in both groups and do not provide a stable direction.

caveats: Likely confounded by age, gender, interests, subculture, and source selection.
findings.evidence_summary: Anime, music, celebrity, and fan-community vocabulary shows a stable topical excess and may help describe corpus composition, not depressive experience.
findings.prompt_guidance: Treat this as a nuisance or stratification feature, never as a clinical semantic cue.

quantitative_support.effect: +0.77 percentage points in average post share

findings.signal: Fandom and pop-culture activity is more prominent among diagnosed users, but functions primarily as a collection or demographic marker.

caveats: Likely reflects demographic, age, interest, temporal, or source-batch differences rather than label causality.
findings.evidence_summary: This is a robust topical-distribution difference: controls contribute more politics/news posts, while diagnosed users show broader but less intensive exposure.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use politics/news mainly to account for collection and activity composition, not as a mental-health indicator.

quantitative_support.effect: Controls have 1.89x the post share overall; diagnosed/control ratio 0.53x
quantitative_support.measure: share of retained posts with politics/news vocabulary
users with at least one politics/news post

findings.signal: Politics and news are substantially more intense in control timelines, despite similar user-level reach.

negative_results: Generic relationships, loneliness, and social-participation vocabulary was nearly ubiquitous and showed little stable separation after post-rate normalization.
Humor/play language did not have a stable direction across folds.
Future-oriented planning was not reduced in diagnosed users; it was slightly more frequent, so lack of future language is not supported as a positive cue.
Mental-health keywords alone were often figurative, quoted, lyrical, humorous, news-related, or third-person and are not specific.
